5. Assume there is an integer n between a and a + 1: a < n < a + 1. Then 0 < n −a < 1.
Thus exists an integer n −a between 0 and 1, a contradiction.
7. proof (by contradiction): Assume there are no integers n such that na ≥b; that is, na < b
for every integer n. Then the set S = {b −na | n ∈Z+} consists of positive integers, so by
the well-ordering principle, S has a least element ℓ. Then ℓ= b −ma for some integer m.
Notice that b −(m + 1)a ∈S, but b −(m + 1)a < b −ma = ℓ, a contradiction.
9. Let A = {a ∈Z | a ≤n0}. Then the set B = {n0 −a | a ∈A} consists of nonnegative in-
tegers and hence has a least element ℓ. Thus, n0 −a ≥ℓfor every element a in A; that
is, n0 −ℓ≥a for every a in A. But n0 −ℓ≤n0, so n0 −ℓ∈A. Thus, n0 −ℓis a largest
element of A.

43. proof: Suppose q(n) satisﬁes the conditions of the second principle. Let p(n) = q(n0) ∧
q(n0 + 1) ∧··· ∧q(n), where n ≥n0. Because q(n0) is true, p(n0) is true. Assume p(k) is

q(k) ∧q(k + 1) is true. So p(k) implies p(k + 1). So by the ﬁrst principle, p(n) is true for
every n ≥n0. Thus, q(n) is true for every n ≥n0.

37. proof (by PMI): When n = 0, LHS = A(2,0) = A(1,1) = A(0,A(1,0)) = 1 + A(1,0) −
1 + A(0,1) = 1 + 2 = 3 = RHS. So P(0) is true.
Assume P(k): A(2,k) = 3 + 2k. Then
A(2,k + 1) = A(1,A(2,k)) = A(1,3 + 2k) = A(0,A(1,2 + 2k)) = 1 + A(1,2 + 2k)
= 1 + A(0,A(1,1 + 2k)) = 2 + A(1,1 + 2k) = 2 + A(0,A(1,2k))
= 3 + A(1,2k) = 3 + (2k + 2) = 3 + 2(k + 1)
Therefore, P(k + 1) is true. Thus, the result follows by induction.
39. proof (by PMI): When n = 0, LHS = A(3,0) = A(2,1) = A(1,A(2,0)) = A(1,3) =

Therefore, P(k + 1) is true. Thus, the result follows by induction.

41. proof: Let x = 2m + 1 and y = 2n + 1 be any two odd integers. Then x + y = (2m + 1) +
(2n + 1) = 2(m + n + 1), an even integer.

43. proof: Let x be an even integer and y an odd integer. Then x = 2m and y = 2n + 1 for
some integers m and n. So x + y = (2m) + (2n + 1) = 2(m + n) + 1, which is an odd
integer.
45. proof (by contradiction): Let x be any integer such that x2 is odd. Suppose x is even,
so x = 2k for some integer k. Then x2 = (2k)2 = 2(2k2), an even integer, which is a
contradiction.
47. proof: Let x = 4m + 1 and y = 4n + 1 be any two integers of the given form. Then
x + y = (4m + 1) + (4n + 1) = 2(2m + 2n + 1), which is an even integer.
49. proof: Let x = 3m + 1 and y = 3n + 1 be any two integers of the given form. Then
x · y = (3m + 1) · (3n + 1) = 3(3mn + m + n) + 1, an integer of the same form.
51. proof: Assume the given conclusion is false. Then both integers are odd, and hence their
product is also odd. This contradicts the given hypothesis, so the result follows.
53. proof: Let n be an even integer, say, n = 2m. Then n2 + n = 4m2 + 2m = 2(2m2 + m),
which is an even integer. On the other hand, let n be an odd integer, say, n = 2m+1. Then
n2 + n = (2m + 1)2 + (2m + 1) = 2(2m2 + 3m + 1), which is also an even integer.
55. proof: Let n be an even integer, say, n = 2m. Then n3 −n = 8m3 −2m = 2(4m2 −m),
which is an even integer. On the other hand, let n be an odd integer, say, n = 2m+1. Then
n3 −n = (2m + 1)3 −(2m + 1) = 2(4m3 + 6m2 + 2m), which is also an even integer.
57. Let A,B, and C be three arbitrary ﬁnite sets. Notice that A ∩C = C ∩A and (A ∩B) ∩
(A ∩C) = A ∩B ∩C.
|A ∪B ∪C| = |A ∪(B ∪C)| = |A| + |B ∪C| −|A ∩(B ∪C)|
= |A| + |B ∪C| −|(A ∩B) ∪(A ∩C)|
= |A| + (|B| + |C| −|B ∩C|) −[|A ∩B| + |A ∩C| −|(A ∩B) ∩(A ∩C)|]
= |A| + |B| + |C| −|A ∩B| −|B ∩C| −|C ∩A| + |A ∩B ∩C|
59. proof: Let n be any positive integer. Then n(n + 1)(n + 2)(n + 3) = [n(n + 3)][(n +
1)(n + 2)] = (n2 + 3n)(n2 + 3n + 2) = (n2 + 3n + 1)2 −1. By Exercise 58, this cannot
be a square.
61. By Exercise 60, 3|(n + 3), so 3|n. Let n = 3m. Then 27m3 + (3m + 1)3 + (3m + 2)3 =
(3m + 3)3. Simplifying, we get 3m3 −2m −1 = 0; that is, (m −1)(3m2 + 3m + 1) = 0.
Since 3m2 + 3m + 1 = 0 has no real solutions, m −1 = 0; that is, m = 1, so n = 3.
63. proof (by PMI): When n = 1, n4 + 2n3 + n2 = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 is divisible by 4. So P(1) is
true. Assume P(k) is true. Let k4 + 2k3 + k2 = 4m for some m ∈Z+. Then
(k + 1)4 + 2(k + 1)3 + (k + 1)2 = (k4 + 2k3 + k2) + 4(k3 + 3k2 + 2k + 1)
= 4m + 4(k3 + 3k2 + 2k + 1) = 4(m + k3 + 3k2 + 2k + 1)
which is divisible by 4. Thus P(k) implies P(k + 1), so the result follows by PMI.

45. proof: Let n and n + 1 be any two consecutive integers that are primes. Because they are
consecutive integers, one of them is even. Suppose it is n. Then 2|n. But n is a prime, so
n = 2 and hence n + 1 = 3. The case that n + 1 is even yields n = 1, a contradiction.

59. proof (by contradiction): Suppose there is a positive integer > 1 that has no prime fac-
tors. Then the set of positive integers that have no prime factors is nonempty, so by the
well-ordering principle, it has a least element n. Because n has no prime factors and n|n,
n cannot be a prime. Let n = ab, where 1 < a,b < n. Since 1 < a < n, a has a prime
factor p. Since p|a and a|n,p|n, which is a contradiction. Thus, every positive integer > 1
has a prime factor.

15. proof: Let d = (m,n),e = ad −bd, and f = (am −bm,an −bn). Because d|m,

(a,b) = 1. So d′ = 1. Thus, (f,a) = 1. Since f|eany, this implies f|e. Thus, e|f and f|e, so

case 1

7. proof: Let d be the ones digit in a. Then a ≡d (mod 10) and a2 ≡d2 (mod 10). Because
a is automorphic, d2 ≡d (mod 10). The only solutions of this congruence are 0, 1, 5 and 6.
9. (by B. D. Beasly) Notice that x,y, and z are relatively prime. Thus, 2 ≤x < y < z. The
given congruences can be combined to get xy + yz + zx −1 ≡0 (mod x,y, and z). Since
x, y, and z are relatively prime, this implies xy + yz + zx ≡1 (mod xyz). Therefore,
xy + yz + zx = 1 + k(xyz) for some positive integer k. This yields 1/x + 1/y + 1/z =
k + 1/xyz > 1. Because 2 ≤x < y < z, this implies (x,y,z) = (2,3,4) or (2,3,5). But
(2,4) ̸= 1, so the unique solution of the given congruences is (2,3,5).
11. (by S. Fernandez) Let (x,y,z) be a solution. Then, by symmetry, a permutation of (x,y,z)
is also a solution. The entries are distinct and are ≥3. Since xy mod z = 2, xy −2 = kz
for some positive integer k. Since y < z, ky < xy −2, so k < x.
Since zx mod y = 2, −2(x + k) ≡(xy −2)x −2k ≡k(zx −2) ≡0 (mod y). So y|2(x + k);
that is, 2(x + k) = ℓy for some positive integer ℓ. Then ℓy = 2(x + k) < 4x < 4y; so
1 ≤ℓ≤3.
Since yz mod x = 2, −2(2+ℓ) ≡2(xy−2)−2ℓ≡2kz−2ℓ≡2(x+k)z−2ℓ≡ℓ(yz−2) ≡
0 (mod x). Therefore, x|2(2 + ℓ).
Thus, y = 2(x + k)

and z = xy −2

ℓ|2(x + k). Of the 22 triplets (ℓ,x,k) that satisfy these conditions, only six yield valid
solutions: (1,3,1), (1,3,2), (2,4,1), (2,4,2), (1,6,1), and (1,6,5). The correspond-

47. Let n be any integer and d its digital root. Then n2 ≡d2 (mod 9). Since 02 ≡0 (mod 9),
(±1)2 ≡1 (mod 9), (±2)2 ≡4 (mod 9), (±3)2 ≡0 (mod 9), and (±4)2 ≡7 (mod 9), it

49. proof: Let N be a triangular number. Then N = n(n + 1)/2 for some positive integer n.
case 1
Let n be even, say, n = 2k. Then N = k(2k + 1). Let d denote the units digit in k.
Then N ≡d(2d + 1) (mod 10). Because 0 ≤d ≤9, the residues of d(2d + 1) modulo 10
are 0, 3, 0, 1, 6, 5, 8, 5, 6, and 1, so the possible units digits are 0, 1, 3, 5, 6, and 8.
case 2
Let n be odd, say, n = 2k + 1. Then N = (k + 1)(2k + 1). Let d denote the
units digit in k. Then N ≡(d + 1)(2d + 1) (mod 10). Since 0 ≤d ≤9, the residues of
(d + 1)(2d + 1) modulo 10 are 3, 0, 1, 6, 5, 8, 5, 6, 1, and 0, so the possible units digits
are 0, 1, 3, 5, 6, and 8.
51. proof: Because Rn = (10n −1)/9, d|Rn implies 10n ≡1 (mod d). Because d|an−1 ...
a1a0,an−110n−1 + an−210n−2 + ··· + a110 + a0 ≡0 (mod d). Therefore, an−110n +
an−210n−1 + ··· + a1102 + a010 ≡0 (mod d); that is, an−210n−1 + an−310n−2 + ··· +
a010 + an−1 ≡0 (mod d), so d|an−2 ...a0an−1. Similarly, d divides the other cyclic
permutations also.
53. proof: Let N = 22000 + 22001 + 22003 + ··· + 22007. Since 23 ≡−1 (mod 9), N =
(23)666 · 22 + (23)667 + (23)667 + (23)667 · 22 + (23)668 + (23)668 · 2 + (23)668 · 22 +
(23)669 ≡(−1)4 + (−1) + (−1)2 + (−1)4 + 1 + 2 + 4 −1 ≡3 (mod 9). So the digital
root of N is 3. But the digital root of a square is 1, 4, 7, or 9. Consequently, N cannot be
a square.

21. We have n ≡0 (mod 3), n ≡−1 (mod 4), n ≡−2 (mod 5), n ≡−3 (mod 6), and n ≡−4
(mod 7). Then n = 3t1 ≡−1 (mod 4), so t1 = 1 + 4t2. Therefore, n = 3(1 + 4t2) =
3 + 12t2 ≡−2 (mod 5), so t2 = 5t3. Then n = 3 + 60t3 ≡−3 (mod 6), which is true
for all t3, so n = 3 + 60t3 ≡−4 (mod 7). This yields t3 = 7t. Therefore, n = 3 + 420t.

23. Let n denote the number of eggs in the basket. Then n ≡1 (mod 2), n ≡2 (mod 3), n ≡3

Then n = 11 + 12(4 + 5t4) = 59 + 60t4 ≡5 (mod 6), which is true for all t4. Therefore,
n = 59 + 60t4 ≡0 (mod 7), so t4 = 1 + t. Thus, n = 59 + 60(1 + 7t) = 119 + 420t, so
there must have been at least 119 eggs in the basket.
25. We have n ≡0 (mod 9), n ≡−1 (mod 16), n ≡−2 (mod 25), and n ≡−3 (mod 49).

(mod 25), so t2 = 15 + 25t3. Then n = 63 + 144(15 + 25t3) = 2223 + 3600t3 ≡−3
(mod 49), so t3 = 14 + 49t. Therefore, n = 2223 + 3600(14 + 49t) = 52623 + 176400t,
so the desired smallest positive integer is 52,623.

49. proof: Let p−1 = 4k, where k ≥1. Let a be a primitive root modulo p, so ordp a = ϕ(p) =
p −1. Then (p −a)ϕ(p) ≡(−a)4k ≡a4k ≡ap−1 ≡1 (mod p), so ordp(p −a)|ϕ(p). Let
ordp(p −a) = h < p −1. Then (p −a)h ≡1 (mod p); that is, (−a)h ≡1 (mod p), so
a2h ≡1 (mod p). Then ordp a|2h; that is, p −1|h. Since (p −1)/2|h and h < p −1,
(p −1)/2 = h = 2k. Thus, h is even. This implies ah ≡(−a)h ≡1 (mod p), where h <
p −1, which is a contradiction.
Conversely, let p−a be a primitive root modulo p. Then ap−1 ≡(−a)p−1 ≡1 (mod p), so
ordp a|p−1. Suppose ordp a = r, where r|p−1, but r < p−1. Since (p−a)2r ≡(−a)2r ≡
(ar)2 ≡1 (mod p), p −1|2r. So (p −1)/2|r. Because (p −1)/2 is even, this implies r is
even. Therefore, (p −a)r ≡(−a)r ≡ar ≡1 (mod p), where r < p −1. Because this is a
contradiction, ordp a = p −1.

fore, ordp(−α)|2k + 1. Let ordp(−α) = t, where t < 2k + 1. Then (−α)t ≡1 (mod p);
that is, αt ≡(−1)t (mod p), so α2t ≡1 (mod p). Then p −1|2t, so (p −1)/2|t, where
t < 2k + 1 = (p −1)/2. Because this is impossible, t = 2k + 1 = (p −1)/2; that is,
ordp(−α) = (p −1)/2.
53. proof: Because α is a primitive root modulo pj,αϕ(pj) ≡1 (mod pj) and αt ̸≡1 (mod pj)
for t < ϕ(pj). Since ϕ(2pj) = ϕ(pj), it follows that αϕ(2pj) ≡1 (mod pj). Because α is
odd, αϕ(2pj) ≡1 (mod 2). Therefore, αϕ(2pj) ≡1 (mod 2pj).
Suppose αe ≡1 (mod 2pj), where e < ϕ(2pj). This implies αe ≡1 (mod pj), where
e < ϕ(p˙j). This contradicts the assumption that α is a primitive root modulo pj. Thus,
α is also a primitive root modulo 2pj.

3. proof: Because p is a prime factor of fn,fn = 22n + 1 ≡0 (mod p). Then 22n ≡−1
(mod p), so 22n+1 ≡1 (mod p). Therefore, ordp 2|2n+1. Let ordp 2 = 2k, where k ≤n.
Then 22k ≡1 (mod p), so 22k·2n−k ≡22n ≡1 (mod p). Because this is impossible,
k = n + 1. Thus, ordp 2 = 2n+1.
5. Because ord19 7 = 3,73 ≡1 (mod 19). Then 83 ≡(7 + 1)3 = 73 + 3 · 72 + 3 · 7 + 1 ≡
1 + 14 + 2 + 1 ≡−1 (mod 19), so 86 ≡1 (mod 19). Thus, ord19 8 = 6.
7. proof: Because p is odd and ordp a = 3, p > 3. Because a3 ≡1 (mod p) and a ̸≡1
(mod p), a2 + a + 1 ≡0 (mod p). Then (a + 1)6 = a6 + 6a5 + 15a4 + 20a3 + 15a2 +
6a + 1 ≡1 + 6a5 + 15a4 + 20a3 + 15a2 + 6a + 1 ≡1 + 21(a2 + a + 1) ≡1 (mod p).
Therefore, ordp(a + 1) = 1, 2, 3, or 6.
case 1
If ordp(a + 1) = 1, then a ≡0 (mod p). This is impossible.
case 2
If ordp(a+1) = 2, then (a+1)2 ≡1 (mod p). This implies a2 +2a ≡0 (mod p),
so p|a or p|a + 2. But p ∤a. So suppose p|a + 2. Because a2 + 2a ≡0 (mod p), a2 + 2 ≡
2(a2 + a + 1) ≡0 (mod p). Therefore, (a2 + a + 1) + 3 ≡(a2 + 2) + (a + 2) (mod p);
that is, 0 + 3 ≡0 + 0 (mod p). Thus, 3 ≡0 (mod p). This is also impossible.
case 3
Let ordp(a + 1) = 3. Then (a + 1)2 ≡1 (mod p), so a3 + 3a2 + 3a ≡0 (mod p);
that is, 3a(a2 + a + 1) ≡2a3 (mod p). This implies 2a3 ≡0 (mod p). Therefore, p|2 or
p|a; both are impossible. Thus, ordp(a + 1) = 6.
9. proof (by C. Vitale): Let (m,n) = (m,10) = (n,10) = 1. Let d = [ordm 10,ordn 10], so
d = x · ordp 10 = y · ordp 10 for some positive integers x and y. Then 10x·ordm 10 ≡10d ≡
1 (mod m) and 10y·ordn 10 ≡10d ≡1 (mod n). This implies 10d ≡1 (mod mn), be-
cause (m,n) = 1. Therefore, ordmn 10|d. But, by deﬁnition, 10ordmn 10 ≡1 (mod mn),
so 10ordmn 10 ≡1 (mod m) and 10ordmn 10 ≡1 (mod n). This implies ordm 10|ordmn 10
and ordn 10|ordmn 10. Therefore, d|ordmn 10. Thus d = [ordm 10,ordn 10] = ordmn 10.

If m ≡−1 (mod 4), then there must be an odd number of prime factors of m that are
congruent to −1 (mod 4); since (−1/p) = −1, by Corollary 11.2 for each such factor, it

23. proof:
By
the
generalized
law
of
quadratic

(m/n)(n/m) =
(−1)(m−1)/2·(n−1)/2. If m ≡1 (mod 4), then (m −1)/2 is even; if n ≡1 (mod 4), then
(n −1)/2 is even. In both cases, (m −1)/2 · (n −1)/2 is even, so (m/n)(n/m) = 1.
Therefore, (n/m) = (m/n).

Therefore, (n/m) = −(m/n).

51. proof: Let α be a solution. Then, by Exercise 50, pn −α is also a solution. Suppose
α ≡pn −α (mod pn). Then 2α ≡0 (mod pn), so α ≡0 (mod pn), which is impossible.
Therefore, α and pn −α are two incongruent solutions.
Let β be any solution of the congruence. Then α2 ≡a ≡β2 (mod pn), so (α + β)
(α −β) = α2 −β2 ≡0 (mod pn). Because n ≥2, this implies either pn|α + β,pn|α −β,
or p|α + β and p|α −β. If pn|α + β, then β = pn −α. If pn|α −β, then α = β. In the last
case, p|2α, so p|α since p is odd. Let α = mp. Then m2p2 ≡a (mod pn), which implies
p|a, which is a contradiction.
Thus, the given congruence has exactly two incongruent solutions, α and pn −α.

is a primitive root modulo q.

55. proof (by contradiction): Assume that there are only a ﬁnite number of such primes,

57. proof: Because p ≡(−1)n + 1 (mod 3), p ≡2 (mod 3) if n is even and 0 (mod 3) oth-
erwise. Therefore, n must be even for p to be a prime; so (p/3) = (2/3) = −1; that is,
3(p−1)/2 ≡32n−1 ≡−1 (mod p). Then 32n ≡1 (mod p).
Let ordp 3 = e. Then e|2n, so e = 2k, where k ≤n. If k < n, then 1 = (32k)2n−k−1 =
32n−1 ≡−1 (mod p), which is a contradiction. Thus ordp 3 = 2n, and 3 is a primitive root
modulo p.
59. proof: Let m ≡1 (mod 4). Then (m −1)/2 is even, so m∗= m. Therefore, (m∗/n) =
(m/n) = (n/m), by Theorem 11.13.
On the other hand, let m ≡3 (mod 4). Then (m −1)/2 is odd. Therefore, (m∗/n) =
(−m/n) = (−1/n)(m/n). If n ≡1 (mod 4), then (−1/n) = 1 and (m/n) = (n/m); thus,
(m∗/n) = 1. (n/m) = (n/m). If n ≡3 (mod 4), then (−1/n) ≡−1 and (m/n) = −(n/m);
thus (m∗/n) = (−1)(−(n/m)) = (n/m).

17. proof (by contradiction): Assume that x4 −y4 = z2 has integral solutions and x–y–z is a
solution with the least positive value of x. Then z2 + y4 = x4; that is, z2 + (y2)2 = (x2)2.
Then z–y2–x2 is a primitive Pythagorean triple.
case 1
Let y2 be odd. Then there exist positive integers m and n such that z = 2mn,
y2 = m2 −n2, and x2 = m2 + n2, where m > n and (m,n) = 1. This implies m4 −n4 =
(m2 + n2)(m2 −n2) = x2y2 = (xy)2, so m–n–xy is also a solution of the given equation.
Because 0 < m2 < m2 +n2 = x2, it follows that m–n–xy is smaller than the least solution,
which is a contradiction.
case 2
Let y2 be even. Then there exist positive integers m and n such that y2 = 2mn,
z2 = m2 −n2, and x2 = m2 + n2, where m > n, (m,n) = 1,m is even, and n is odd. Be-
cause (2m,n) = 1 and y2 = 2mn, 2m = r2 and n = s2 for some integers r and s. Because
r is even, this implies m = 2t2 for some integer t. Therefore, x2 = 4t4 + s4, so 2t2–s2–x
is a primitive Pythagorean triple. Consequently, there are positive integers u and v such
that 2t2 = 2uv, s2 = u2 −v2, and x = u2 + v2, where u > v and (u,v) = 1. Since t2 = uv,
u = a2 and v = b2 for some integers a and b. Then s2 = a4 −b4, so a–b–s is also a solu-
tion of the given equation x4 −y4 = z2. Because 0 < a = √u < u2 + v2 = x, this yields a
contradiction. Thus, the given equation has no positive integral solutions.

17. Let x −1, x, x + 1, and x + 2 be the four consecutive integers. Then (x −1)3 + x3 +
(x + 1)3 = (x + 2)3. Simplifying, we get (x −4)(x2 + x + 1) = 0. Because x2 + x + 1 = 0

5. Let x and y be any two even integers. Then x = 2m and y = 2n for some integers m and n.
Then x + y = 2m + 2n = 2(m + n), which is also an even integer.
7. Let x = 2m be any even integer. Then x2 = (2m)2 = 2(2m2) is also an even integer.
9. Let x be any odd integer. Then x = 2m + 1 for some integer m. Then x2 = (2m + 1)2 =
2(2m2 + 2m) + 1, which is an odd integer.
11. Let x be any even integer and y any odd integer. Then x = 2m and y = 2n + 1 for some
integers m and n. Then xy = (2m)(2n + 1) = 2(2mn + m), an even integer.
13. Let x = 4k +1. Then x2 = (4k +1)2 = 16k2 +8k +1 = 4(4k2 +2k)+1 = 4m+1, where
m = 4k2 + 2k is an even integer. Therefore, x2 is also an integer of the same form.
15. Let x be any integer. Assume it is not even, so it is odd and is of the form 2m + 1. Then
x2 = (2m + 1)2 = 4m2 + 4m + 1 = 2(2m2 + 2m) + 1, which is an odd integer. So, the
given hypothesis is false and the result follows.
17. Let x and y be any two integers. Assume that the given conclusion is false; that is, assume
that both x and y are odd integers. Then x = 2m + 1 and y = 2n + 1 for some integers m
and n, so xy = (2m + 1)(2n + 1) = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1, an odd integer. This negates the
given hypothesis and so the result follows.
19. Suppose
√
2 is not an irrational number; that is,
√
2 is a rational number. Let
√
2 = a/b,
where a and b have no positive common factors except 1. Then (a/b)2 = 2 or a2 = 2b2.
Therefore, 2 is a factor of a2 and hence of a. Then a = 2m for some integer m. So (2m)2 =
2b2 or b2 = 2m2. Then 2 is a factor of b2 and hence of b. Consequently, 2 is a common
factor of a and b, which is a contradiction.
21. Assume √p is a rational number a/b, where a and b have no positive common factors
except 1. Then √p = a/b,(a/b)2 = p, or a2 = pb2. Consequently, p is a factor of a2 and
hence of a. So let a = mp. Then (mp)2 = pb2 or b2 = pm2. As before, this shows p is a
factor of b. Thus, p is a common factor of a and b, a contradiction.
23. proof: case 1 Let n be an even integer, say, 2m. Then n2 +n = (2m)2 +2m = 2(2m2 +m),
an even integer.
case 2 Let n be an odd integer, say, 2m + 1. Then n2 + n = (2m + 1)2 + (2m + 1) =
(4m2 + 4m + 1) + (2m + 1) = 2(2m2 + 3m + 1), again, an even integer.
25. proof: Every integer n is of the form 3k,3k + 1, or 3k + 2.
case 1 Let n = 3k. Then n3 −n = (3k)3 −(3k) = 27k3 −3k = 3(9k3 −k).
case 2 Let n = 3k + 1. Then n3 −n = (3k + 1)3 −(3k + 1) = (27k3 + 27k2 + 9k + 1) −
(3k + 1) = 27k3 + 27k2 + 6k = 3(9k3 + 9k2 + 2k).
case 3 Let n = 3k + 2. Then n3 −n = (3k + 2)3 −(3k + 2) = (27k3 + 54k2 + 36k + 8) −
(3k + 2) = 27k3 + 54k2 + 33k + 6 = 3(9k3 + 18k2 + 11k + 2)
Thus, in every case, n3 −n is divisible by 3.

(a + x) + c = b + c; that is, (a + c) + x = b + c. Therefore, a + c < b + c.
